core.text: To tell what *was happening* or *used to happen*, Latin slips *-ba-* between the stem and the person endings: **the imperfect (the 'was doing' tense)**. *amā-ba-t* — he was loving, he loved (over a stretch of time); *habitā-ba-nt* — they were living. The endings are *-bam, -bās, -bat, -bāmus, -bātis, -bant*; the first person uses *-m*, not *-ō*. The 1st and 2nd conjugations add *-ba-* straight to the stem vowel (*amābat, vidēbat*); the 3rd and 4th put an *-ē-* first (*scrībēbat, dormiēbat*). Latin name: imperfectum indicātīvī āctīvī.
The English past has several shapes: *I walked* (one event), *I was walking* (in progress), *I used to walk* (habit). The imperfect covers the last two.
Stem (+ ē for the 3rd and 4th) + ba + -m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt.

invented.en: The boys were playing in the garden.

core.text: Both are past. The imperfect *amābat* paints a state or habit — he loved her, was loving her; the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense) *amāvit* reports a finished event — he fell in love. Setting is imperfect; what happened next is perfect. Look for *-ba-* against a perfect stem (*-v-, -s-, -u-*).

more.text: *-bā-* is long before *-s, -mus, -tis* (*amābās, amābāmus*) and short before *-m, -t, -nt*. It is the tense of background, habit and the setting of a story. Besides *was doing*, it can mean *began to* or *tried to* (*clāmābat* — began to shout) and is the tense of description in a narrative. The imperfect of *esse* is *eram*: see the irregular imperfect.

The learner's notes (week 19): Latin shows tense with an intermediate ending between the stem and the person ending; the imperfect is one of three past tenses, for ongoing or repeated action and for setting the scene for the main events (*I was walking down the street, when…*; *I used to walk…*); the marker *(e)ba* loses its *e* after *a-* and *e-*stems and keeps it after *(i)-* and *i-*stems (*pōnēbam, pulsābam, vidēbam, fugiēbam, veniēbam*); the person endings lose their variable vowels after the *a*, and the first person always uses *-m*.

Ørberg (chapter XIX): tempus praeteritum, 3rd person *-bat / -bant*, *-ēbat / -ēbant*; *computābat, pārēbat, scrībēbat, dormiēbat*; *ante vīgintī annōs Iūlius in lūdō dormiēbat, male computābat, foedē scrībēbat*. A&G §470–471 list the uses: continued action, repeated action, description, and the 'was beginning to' sense.

teach.title: What the tense does
teach.say: When Latin looks back at the past it can report one finished event, or it can paint what was going on. For what was going on — and for what went on again and again — it uses the imperfect (the 'was doing' tense). *Iūlius ambulābat* is not 'Julius walked once' but 'Julius was walking', and *Iūlius cotīdiē ambulābat* is 'Julius used to walk every day'. The sign of it is *-bā-* sitting between the verb's stem and its person ending.

check.ask: Tap the verb that says what Marcus used to do every day.

teach.title: The stem, then -bā-, then -t
teach.say: Build the word in three pieces. Take the stem *ambulā-*, add *-bā-*, then add the ending that says who: *-t* for he, she or it, *-nt* for they. Before a final *-t* or *-nt* that long *ā* shortens, which is why you write *ambulā-ba-t* and *clāmā-ba-nt*. A verb of the second conjugation (the conjugation is which of the four families a Latin verb belongs to; the second is the *-ēre* family) does exactly the same on its own stem vowel: *tacē-* gives *tacēbat*. Nothing else in the word changes.

show.say: ambulābat, ambulābant — stem, then -bā-, then -t or -nt

check.ask: Now the same two cells on another verb: write the imperfect of cantō for 'he' and for 'they'.

teach.title: The other persons, and -m for 'I'
teach.say: The remaining persons put the ordinary endings on that same *-bā-*: *-s* for you, *-mus* for we, *-tis* for you all. The one thing to remember is the 'I' form: it ends in *-m*, not in the *-ō* the present uses. So *ambulō* 'I am walking' but *ambulābam* 'I was walking'.

check.ask: Write the imperfect of laudō for I, for you, for we and for you all.

teach.title: The 3rd and 4th conjugations put -ē- first
teach.say: Third- and fourth-conjugation verbs have no long vowel of their own to carry the marker, so they slip in an *-ē-* before it: *mitt-* becomes *mittēbat*, *audi-* becomes *audiēbant*. Read the word as stem + ē + bā + ending. The *-bā-* is the same as before; only the joining vowel is new.

show.say: mittēbat, mittēbant — stem, then ē, then bā

check.ask: Now the same two cells on scrībō: the imperfect for 'he' and for 'they'.

teach.title: Telling it from the present
teach.say: The present (the 'is doing' tense) and the imperfect differ by those two letters and nothing else: *rīdet* 'she is laughing' against *rīdēbat* 'she was laughing', *pōnit* 'he puts' against *pōnēbat* 'he was putting'. Cover the ending and look for *-ba-* or *-bā-*: if it is there, the sentence has moved into the past.

check.ask: Tap the one verb here that has moved into the past.

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: Now write one. The imperfect keeps the background running while everything else happens inside it, so two imperfects often sit in the same sentence: *Iūlius pecūniam vidēbat et in sacculō pōnēbat*. Watch the order too — Latin is happy to put the verb before its subject, so do not expect the last word of a sentence to be the verb.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the imperfect of scrībō, third person singular.
